audit.method: Amal repeats Medi's sentence within 25s sharing at least 40% of his Arabic words; the changed words are the correction. Classified by rule, never guessed.

rules.name: el- (the)
rules.one_line: `el-` marks a thing you already know; nothing marks a new one.
rules.why: English has 'a' and 'the'. Arabic only has 'the' - leaving it off is how you say 'a'.
more: The sun-letter half: before s, sh, t, d, r, n, z, l the l disappears and the next letter doubles.
el-shams is written with an l but said esh-shams.
el-dar -> ed-dar.  el-nas -> en-nas.  el-rajol -> er-rajol.
Moon letters keep the l: el-bait, el-kalb, el-walad.

rules.name: idafa (possession)
rules.one_line: Thing first, owner second - and the first word never takes `el-`.
rules.why: There is no word for 'of'. You just put the two nouns next to each other.
more: el-bait Medi is always wrong - the first noun drops el-.
The LAST noun decides whether the whole phrase is definite.
bait m3allem = a teacher's house.  bait el-m3allem = the teacher's house.

rules.name: feminine -t in idafa
rules.one_line: A feminine first word grows a `-t` before the owner.
rules.why: The hidden -a ending on feminine nouns wakes up as -t when something follows it.
more: 8urfe room -> 8urfet el-noam the bedroom.
madrase school -> madraset el-walad the boy's school.
Only feminine nouns do this. bait Medi stays plain.

rules.name: possessive endings
rules.one_line: Stick the owner on the end of the word.
rules.why: Instead of 'my name', Arabic says 'name-my' as one word.
more: The set: -i my, -ak your (m), -ek your (f), -o his, -ha her, -na our, -kom your (pl), -hom their.
baiti my house, baitha her house, baithom their house.

rules.name: chain possession
rules.one_line: Stack three or more nouns; only the last can take `el-`.
rules.why: Same rule as A2, just longer - every noun except the last stays bare.
more: muftaa7 bab el-bait = the key of the door of the house.
You never put el- on muftaa7 or bab - only on el-bait.

rules.name: professions
rules.one_line: Job titles are idafa too - watch where `el-` lands.
rules.why: A job made of two words follows A2 exactly.
more: doktoar snaan = a tooth-doctor, no el- anywhere = 'a dentist'.
m3allem el-3arabi = the Arabic teacher - el- only on the second word.

rules.name: noun + adjective
rules.one_line: Adjective goes AFTER. Where `el-` sits changes sentence vs phrase.
rules.why: One el- = a full sentence. Two el- = just a name for a thing.
more: el-bait 7elu is a complete sentence - no word for 'is' needed (see C1).
el-bait el-7elu is not a sentence, it's a label. It leaves you waiting for more.
bait 7elu = a pretty house.

rules.name: gender on adjectives
rules.one_line: Feminine noun takes a feminine adjective.
rules.why: Adjectives change shape to match the noun - usually by adding -a or -e.
more: akel zaaki tasty food (m), akle zaakye a tasty dish (f).
If the noun ends in -a/-e it is almost always feminine.

rules.name: plurals
rules.one_line: Some add an ending, many change shape, and two has its own form.
rules.why: Arabic has three plurals: regular endings, irregular reshapes, and a special 'exactly two'.
more: Regular: -een (people, m) and -aat (things/f) - muwazzaf -> muwazzafeen.
Irregular: you memorise them - bait->byoot, bab->bwaab, shubbak->shababeek.
Exactly two: add -ein - yom->yomein, saa3a->saa3tain.

rules.name: demonstrative keeps el-
rules.one_line: The noun after hada / hadi / hadol keeps its `el-`.
rules.why: Keep the el- and it is a phrase. Drop it and you just made a sentence.
more: hada el-ktab la-Mehdi = this book is Mehdi's.
hadi el-moazeh = this banana. hadi moazeh = this is a banana.
Superlatives are the exception - they never take el-: hadi a2al akleh.

rules.name: hada / hadi
rules.one_line: This-and-that words must match the gender.
rules.why: Pick the form by the gender of the thing you are pointing at.
more: Near: hada (m), hadi (f), hadol (plural).
Far: hadaak (m), hadeek (f).
Common slip: using hada for a feminine noun.
rules.tally_title: hada (m) / hadi (f) must match the noun

rules.name: broken plurals are patterns
rules.one_line: The irregular plurals repeat the same few shapes - learn the mould, not 200 words.
rules.why: Her Doc lists each plural as its own word, so the repeating shapes are easy to miss.
more: byoot / swaa2 / 3yoon all share one mould.
bwaab / twaab share another.
shababeek / masaajed / makaateb share a third.
Not in her Docs as a lesson - this is a gap.

rules.name: kul: all vs every
rules.one_line: `kul` + `el-` = all of it. `kul` alone = every.
rules.why: One little el- flips the whole meaning.
more: kul el-zlaam = all the men (a specific group).
kul zalame = every man (each one separately).
el-kul on its own = everybody.

rules.name: present with b-
rules.one_line: Every ordinary present verb starts with b-.
rules.why: The b- is the marker that says 'this is a normal present-tense verb'.
more: ana ba-, inta bti-, inti bti-..i, huwwe bi-, heyye bti-, i7na bni-, intu bti-..u, humme bi-..u.
Drop the b- only in the cases listed in B2, B3 and B4.

rules.name: b-drop after modals
rules.one_line: No b- after want/must/can words.
rules.why: The first word already carries the tense, so the second verb goes bare.

laazem aru7 I have to go - never laazem baru7.

rules.name: the drop carries down a chain
rules.one_line: Once dropped, it stays dropped across u / aw / wala.
examples: I want to drink and eat
rules.why: The second and third verbs stay bare as long as the person doing them hasn't changed.
more: laazem aru7 u ashuf u arja3 - all three bare.
A new subject ends the chain: laazem aru7 u huwwe biji - biji gets its b- back.

rules.name: when the b- comes back
rules.one_line: The b- returns the moment you leave the want/must clause.
examples: I think that he doesn't like us
rules.why: B2 and B3 take the b- away. This is the rule that puts it back.
more: enno starts a real new sentence, so the b- returns.
A full stop restarts it too.
Any clause stating a real fact rather than a wish keeps it: 3endo tilfizion ma byista5demo.
Inside the gatekeeper's reach even a pointer verb stays bare.

rules.name: past tense
rules.one_line: Endings on the back of the verb say who did it.
rules.why: No b-, no prefix - the past is all endings.
more: -et I, -et you (m), -ti you (f), nothing for he, -et she, -na we, -tu you (pl), -u they.
Amal's Doc has all 8 persons for each verb - 825 rows.

rules.name: kaan = was / were
rules.one_line: Arabic has no 'was' in the present, but it does in the past.
rules.why: C1 says you skip 'am/is/are'. In the past you must put kaan back.
more: ana ta3baan I am tired -> kunt ta3baan I was tired.
kunt I, kaan he, kaanat she, kunna we, kaanu they.

rules.name: kaan + b-verb = used to
rules.one_line: Habitual past - something you did regularly.
rules.why: kaan plus a normal b-verb means it happened over and over back then.
more: Note the b- STAYS here - this is not a drop case.
kaan bishrab ahwe kul yom he used to drink coffee every day.

rules.name: bakoon / ykoon
rules.one_line: No 'to be' in the plain present, but you need it after lamma/iza and for habits.
rules.why: This is the 'being' verb that appears only in certain slots.
more: Plain now: drop it - ana ta3baan.
After lamma / iza: you must use it - lamma akoon, iza bikoon.
For habits and the future: bakoon ta3baan ba3ed el-shu8el.
rules.tally_title: bakoon / ykoon: right person, and 'being' vs 'becoming'

rules.name: commands
rules.one_line: Telling someone to do something.
rules.why: Strip the present prefix and you're usually most of the way there.
more: btishrab you drink -> ishrab drink!
Feminine adds -i: ishrabi. Plural adds -u: ishrabu.
Amal's Doc has 107 rows of these.

rules.name: negative commands
rules.one_line: `ma` or `la` in front of the YOU-form.
rules.why: You don't negate the command form - you negate the 'you do' form.
more: Not ma ishrab - you need ma tishrab.
Feminine: ma tishrabi. Plural: ma tishrabu.
Amal drills this heavily - 202 hits across 9 of your lessons.

rules.name: make-X vs get-X
rules.one_line: Doubling the middle letter turns 'I become' into 'I make someone'.
rules.why: One is about you, the other is about what you do to somebody else.
more: bad7ak I laugh -> bada77ek I make people laugh.
baz3al I get sad -> baza33el I make someone sad.
bazha2 I get bored -> bazahhe2 I bore people.
7 pairs in her Doc, plus ba3asseb.
rules.tally_title: Make-X vs get-X verb pairs: babse6 / banbese6, baz3ej / banze3ej

rules.name: future with ra7
rules.one_line: `ra7` plus a bare verb.
rules.why: ra7 does the work of 'will' / 'going to'.
more: The verb after ra7 drops its b- (this is a B3 case).
ra7 aru7 I'll go - never ra7 baru7.

rules.name: 3am = right now
rules.one_line: `3am` plus a verb means it's happening this second.
rules.why: English uses -ing for both habits and right-now. Arabic splits them.
more: bashrab ahwe = I drink coffee (generally).
3am bashrab ahwe = I'm drinking coffee right now.
Amal has said this only 3 times in your recorded lessons.

rules.name: participles
rules.one_line: State words that act like adjectives.
rules.why: Not really a verb - it describes the state you're in.
more: raaye7 going, naasi having forgotten, 3aaref knowing, saaken living.
They take gender: raaye7 (m) / raay7a (f).
Only 1 hit in all your lessons - this is your thinnest bucket.

rules.name: kan laazem
rules.one_line: `kaan` stacked on `laazem` = had to / should have.
rules.why: B6 kaan plus B2 laazem, together - and the b- still drops.
more: kaan laazem aru7 I had to go - never kaan laazem baru7.
Negative flips the meaning to regret: ma kaan laazem a7ki I shouldn't have spoken.
Amal corrected you on this live on Aug 25.

rules.name: saarli
rules.one_line: 'It's been X for me' - duration up to now.
rules.why: Takes the PERSON ending, not a separate subject word.
more: saarli me, saarlak you (m), saarlek you (f), saarlo him, saarlha her.
saarli sitt shhoor bat3allam 3arabi - I've been learning Arabic for six months.
From your Sep 21 lesson: min saarlha inta akaltha?

rules.name: no word for 'to be'
rules.one_line: Arabic drops am / is / are in the plain present.
rules.why: You just put the two parts side by side. Nothing goes between them.
more: huwwe doktoar - he is a doctor.
Put kaan back for the past (B6) and ykoon after lamma/iza (B8).

rules.name: the pointer rule
rules.one_line: Move the object to the front and the verb grows an ending pointing back.
rules.why: The -h on the end is the 'it' you already mentioned at the front.
more: el-akel illi taba5to - the food that I cooked; -o points back to the food.
Endings: -o him/it, -ha her/it (f), -hom them.
Forgetting the ending is one of your recorded slips.
rules.tally_title: Pointer pronoun -o / -ha after a fronted object

rules.name: comparatives
rules.one_line: `a7san`, `aktar`, `a2al` - and never `el-` in front.
rules.why: The same word covers 'better' and 'best'. Context tells you which.
more: a7san better/best, aktar more/most, a2al less/least, aswa2 worse/worst.
Never el-a7san - that's the recorded slip.
rules.tally_title: No el- on aktar / a7san + eshi

rules.name: saying no
rules.one_line: `ma` before verbs, `mish` before nouns and adjectives.
rules.why: Two different 'not' words, picked by what comes after.
more: Verb -> ma: ma baru7 I don't go.
Adjective or noun -> mish: mish zaaki not tasty.
Never: abadan ma baru7 I never go.

rules.name: words that drag a ma along
rules.one_line: `abadan` is not enough on its own - the verb still needs `ma`.
rules.why: Two different -ma's that pull opposite ways on the b-.
more: abadan ma baru7 - keeps the b-, because abadan is real negation.
abel-ma yiju (before they come) - that -ma is part of the conjunction, not negation.
ba3ed-ma teshra7i (after you explain) - same, and the b- drops.

rules.name: u / aw / wala
rules.one_line: and, either-or, nor/nothing.
rules.why: Three small joining words that don't overlap the way English 'or' does.
more: u = and.  aw = or (a real choice).  wala = nor / not even / none.
wala 7ada nobody, wala ishi nothing.
Mixing up aw and wala is a recorded slip.

events.recast: ولا is used more for options

rules.name: iza / lamma
rules.one_line: if, when - and both change the verb after them.
rules.why: They trigger the b-drop (B3) and often need ykoon (B8).
more: lamma = when (it will happen).  iza = if (it might).
lamma aru7 when I go - bare verb.
lamma akoon ta3baan when I'm tired - needs ykoon.

rules.name: illi
rules.one_line: 'the one that' - never changes shape.
rules.why: One word covers that / which / who, for everything.
more: It never changes for gender or number.
The clause after it usually needs the C2 pointer ending - ishtareto not ishtarait.

rules.name: question words
rules.one_line: The basic set.
rules.why: Arabic doesn't need a 'do' helper - the question word just goes first.
more: shu what, wein where, keef how, 2addesh how much, kam how many, lesh why, meen who, aymta when.

rules.name: word order
rules.one_line: Normal is verb then object; front the object and C2 kicks in.
rules.why: Moving something to the front is allowed - but then you owe a pointer ending.
more: Plain: verb, then what it acts on.
Fronted: the thing first, then the verb WITH its ending.

rules.name: preposition goes in front
rules.one_line: English leaves it dangling; Arabic never does.
examples: where did you buy it from?
rules.why: The preposition fuses to the question word and leads the sentence.
more: min wein from where, lawein to where, 3an shu about what.
ma3 meen with who, min emta since when, min shu from what.
Amal taught this out loud on Sep 16: lawein - we add it to the question, always.

rules.name: prepositions
rules.one_line: Small words with several jobs each.
rules.why: Each one covers 2-4 English prepositions, so you learn them by use, not translation.
more: min from, 3ala on/about, fi in, ma3 with, bi by/with, la to/for.
3ala alone covers on, about, against and owing.

rules.name: verb + its fixed preposition
rules.one_line: The verb chooses it. You can't guess from English.
rules.why: Learn the verb and its preposition as one unit.
more: ba6lub min - ask FROM (not 'to').
5aayef min - scared FROM (not 'of').
mishtaa2 la missing TO, 2al2aan 3ala worried ON, mu5talef 3an different FROM.
Zero hits in your lessons - nobody has drilled this set.

rules.name: preposition keeps el-
rules.one_line: Where English drops 'the', Levantine keeps it.
rules.why: English says 'from home' and 'by car' with no 'the'. Arabic puts it back.
more: bi / la / fi fuse with it: bi-l..., la-l..., fi-l...
min / 3ala / ma3 keep it separate: min el-bait, 3ala el-6aawle.
No el- on a name (la-Mehdi, fi America), on something already owned (ma3i, ma3 sadiqi), or when it really is indefinite (ma3 3aseer).

rules.name: endings on prepositions
rules.one_line: Stick the person on the end of the preposition.
rules.why: Same idea as A4, but on prepositions instead of nouns.
more: ma3i with me, ma3ak with you, ma3o with him.
minni from me, minnak from you, minno from him.
Some double their letter: min -> minno, not mino.

rules.name: endings on verbs
rules.one_line: The object rides on the back of the verb.
rules.why: A different set from D3 - these attach straight to the verb.
more: shufo see him, shufha see her, shufhom see them.
bi7kili he tells me, bi7kilak he tells you.
Feeds the C2 pointer rule.

rules.name: iyyaa - the second object
rules.one_line: A verb carries only one pronoun; a second one rides on `iyyaa`.
rules.why: You cannot stack two object endings on one verb, so the second gets its own word.
more: ba36ii-k = I give you. ba36ii-k iyyaa = I give it to you.
jeeb-li = bring me. jeeb-li iyyaa = bring it to me.
Absent from both her Docs - confirmed against the live Doc 2026-09-22.

rules.name: number + noun
rules.one_line: 2 has its own form; 3-10 take a plural; 11+ take a SINGULAR.
rules.why: The rule flips twice as the number gets bigger - this is the part English never prepares you for.
more: Exactly 2: no number word, just the -ein ending - yomein, saa3tain.
3 to 10: number + plural noun - talat iyyaam, 5ams saa3aat.
11 and up: number + SINGULAR noun - 7da3sh yom, 3ishreen saa3a.

candidates.why: 11 and up takes a singular noun

rules.name: clock time
rules.one_line: `el-saa3a` + the feminine number.
rules.why: You say 'the hour three and a half', not 'three thirty'.
more: u noss and a half, u rube3 and a quarter, illa rube3 quarter to.
u talateen and thirty, for exact minutes.

rules.name: time units, two-of and many-of
rules.one_line: Each unit has three forms.
rules.why: One, exactly two, and many - the middle one is the A9 dual.
more: saa3a / saa3tain / saa3aat - hour.
yom / yomein / iyyaam - day.
shahr / shahrein / shhoor - month.

rules.name: calendar
rules.one_line: Days, months, and 'on Monday'.
rules.why: Days are just 'day the-second', 'day the-third' and so on.
more: el-itnein Monday (day 2), el-talaata Tuesday, el-arb3a Wednesday.
el-jum3a Friday, el-sabet Saturday, el-a7ad Sunday.

rules.name: the seven hard letters
rules.one_line: Sounds English doesn't have - scored as pronunciation, not grammar.
rules.why: Dropping them makes a different word, or no word at all.
more: 2 = hamza glottal stop, 3 = ayn, 7 = ha, 5 = kha, 6 = ta, 8 = ghayn, 9 = sad.
Your recorded slips are mostly ayn, ta and ghayn.

rules.name: vowel length
rules.one_line: Holding a vowel longer changes the word.
rules.why: Arabic treats a long vowel and a short one as two different letters.
more: Written Arabic doesn't mark short vowels, so this can only be judged by ear.
In Arabizi a doubled letter means hold it: saam vs sam.

rules.name: shadda (doubled letter)
rules.one_line: Hold the consonant twice as long.
rules.why: It's the difference between B12's two verb types - audio only, never judged from spelling.
more: sakar sugar vs sakkar he closed.
In B12 the doubling IS the grammar: bad7ak vs bada77ek.
